References / Painting / 242

Marilyn Diptych

Andy Warhol’s fifty repeated Marilyn Monroe heads on two canvases: a grid in flat color on the left, fading black and white on the right.

Source
Tate: ‘Marilyn Diptych’, Andy Warhol, 1962
Creator
Andy Warhol
Made
1962
Style
Pop art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Repetitive, commercial, elegiac
Evidence
Tate serves images of this work only up to 256 px wide; larger sizes return HTTP 403. The 256 px image confirms only the two-panel grid, which is too small for observation. Description relies on Tate’s record and Wikipedia.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Tate gives the medium as alkyd ink, acrylic paint, oil ground, and graphite on two canvases. Tate.

Warhol made the work in 1962, shortly after Monroe’s death in August. It repeats fifty images from a publicity still for the 1953 film Niagara by Gene Kornman: colored portraits on the left panel and fading black-and-white impressions on the right. Tate acquired it in 1980. Wikipedia.

Warhol described silkscreening as picking a photograph, blowing it up, transferring it in glue onto silk, and rolling ink across it, so that each image is the same but slightly different. Wikipedia.

A later screenprint of the same head is Marilyn Monroe (Marilyn).

Why it belongs

The diptych gives the style its second layout: not one enlarged panel but a strict grid of identical units, like goods on a shelf or frames on a contact sheet.

The contrast between the two panels depends on print variation. On screen, the equivalent is a grid in which units vary slightly in ink density or registration.

Borrow

Repeat one image in a tight grid with no gutters, and vary only its color or density from cell to cell.

Pair a colored grid with a monochrome grid of the same unit.
